The report names Walmart, Thermo Fisher Scientific, PepsiCo, Microsoft, Lowe’s, Apple, Alphabet, T-Mobile, Amazon and other securities; each transaction is shown with a reported value range rather than an exact proceeds figure. This card isolates those disclosed transactions from Howard Lutnick’s later sales under an ethics agreement. The disclosure establishes that transactions were reported on that date, but it does not establish why each sale was made, whether tariff information played any role or whether the trades produced a particular gain or loss. It provides no basis to treat the sales as insider trading or to attribute them to a specific policy announcement. No finding of misconduct is supplied. The entry records the disclosure and its timing, while leaving motive and any connection to government information unresolved.

children.title: Lutnick’s Newmark Divestiture Followed His Ethics Agreement
children.description_short: Howard Lutnick began selling Newmark holdings under an ethics agreement in May 2025 and completed the divestiture in October.
children.description_medium: Newmark’s SEC filing says Howard Lutnick agreed on May 16, 2025, to sell company shares as part of divestment required under his ethics agreement. It reports initial closings in May and completion on October 6. The filing identifies ethics compliance as the purpose; it does not establish a connection to tariff information.
children.description_long: Newmark Group’s annual filing to the SEC reports that Howard Lutnick agreed on May 16, 2025, to sell 10,969,533 Newmark Class A shares he beneficially owned. The filing says the first closing, for 10,839,674 shares held by Lutnick, his spouse and trusts, occurred May 19; a further 129,859 retirement-account shares were tied to later regulatory closing conditions. It states these transactions were pursuant to Lutnick’s agreement to divest company interests to comply with U.S. government ethics rules connected to his appointment as Commerce secretary. Newmark then reported that he completed his divestiture on October 6 and no longer had voting or dispositive power over the company’s securities. This is a separate ethics-agreement divestiture, distinct from Pete Hegseth’s March 24 transaction report. The filing does not connect Lutnick’s sales to tariff information or suggest they were pre-announcement trades. The record therefore describes a disclosed compliance process and does not treat the divestitures as evidence of opportunistic trading.

source_fact_map.quote: On May 16, 2025, Mr. Howard Lutnick, the U.S. Secretary of Commerce and the Company’s former Executive Chairman and former Chairman of the Board, agreed to sell to the Company 10,969,533 shares of Newmark Class A common stock beneficially owned by him
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: On May 16, 2025, Mr. Howard Lutnick, the U.S. Secretary of Commerce and the Company’s former Executive Chairman and former Chairman of the Board, agreed to sell to the Company 10,969,533 shares of Newmark Class A common stock beneficially owned by him, including (i) 7,989,936 shares held directly by Mr. Lutnick, (ii) 2,843,781 shares held in Mr. Lutnick’s personal asset trust, (iii) 3,384 shares held by the Mr. Howard Lutnick Family Trust, (iv) 2,573 shares held by Mr. Lutnick’s spouse, and (v) 129,859 shares originating from retirement accounts, including certain shares held by Mr. Lutnick’s spouse. The closing of the sale of the 10,839,674 shares held by him, his spouse, and the trusts occurred on May 19, 2025, and the closing of the sale of 129,859 shares held in retirement accounts will occur immediately after the closing of the sale of the voting shares of CFGM by Mr. Lutnick, which are pending subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions, including receipt of required regulatory approvals. These transactions are pursuant to Mr. Howard Lutnick’s agreement to divest his interests in the Company to comply with U.S. government ethics rules in connection with his appointment as the U.S. Secretary of Commerce. On October 6, 2025, Mr. Howard Lutnick, the U.S. Secretary of Commerce and the Company’s former Executive Chairman and former Chairman of the Company’s Board, completed his previously announced divestiture of his holdings in the Company in connection with his appointment as the U.S. Secretary of Commerce. Mr. Howard Lutnick no longer has any voting or dispositive power over any of the securities of the Company.

title: June Report Describes FBI Personnel Actions Against Senior Agents
description_short: June 2025 reporting described FBI personnel actions involving senior agents and a top deputy.
description_medium: Reporting dated June 5, 2025 described FBI leadership forcing two veteran agents out and disciplining a third employee. The New York Times named Spencer Evans, Stanley Meador and Michael Feinberg; its account attributed details to people familiar with the matter. The reporting supports a narrow FBI personnel episode, not the frozen claim that Defense and Intelligence Community inspectors general were fired in June.
description_long: The New York Times reported on June 5, 2025, that the FBI targeted several employees in personnel actions. Its article said two veteran agents in Virginia were forced out and another employee in Las Vegas was punished, citing people familiar with the matter. The report named Spencer Evans and Stanley Meador as senior agents who ran field offices in Las Vegas and Richmond, and Michael Feinberg as a top deputy in Norfolk. The article’s summary says an agent threatened with demotion opted to resign while two others were forced to move and retire; it does not identify each consequence with each named person in the excerpts accessed here. The Times placed the episode among transfers, ousters and demotions as Kash Patel reshaped the bureau. It reported that current and former agents characterized the broader changes as retaliation; that is an attributed view, not a legal finding. The available reporting supports a narrow June FBI personnel account. It does not support the frozen record’s claims that Defense or Intelligence Community inspectors general were removed or that these actions eliminated the last internal checks. The January inspector-general report previously linked to the record concerns a separate event.

research_attempts.detail: AP reported about 17 IG dismissals beginning Friday Jan 24 and effective immediately; this is a different January event and not used for June facts.

uncertainties: The New York Times account relies on people familiar with personnel decisions; it is not a court or agency finding of retaliation.
The source excerpt does not associate every named person with each consequence, and precise effective dates are not established.
No source reviewed supports June removals of Defense Department or Intelligence Community inspectors general, or the claim that the actions eliminated the last internal checks.
insight_facts: June reporting described FBI personnel actions affecting two veteran agents and another employee.
The report names Spencer Evans, Stanley Meador and Michael Feinberg.
Retaliation is an attributed characterization, not an adjudicated finding.
unknown_fields: individual assignment of every reported consequence
any June inspector-general dismissals at Defense or the Intelligence Community

evidence_map.fact: A June 5 New York Times report described two veteran agents being forced out and another FBI employee being punished, based on people familiar with the matter.
evidence_map.quote: The F.B.I. has targeted another round of employees who ran afoul of conservatives, forcing out two veteran agents in Virginia —one of whom is friends with a critic of President Trump —and punishing another in Las Vegas, according to several people familiar with the matter.
evidence_map.source_excerpt: The F.B.I. has targeted another round of employees who ran afoul of conservatives, forcing out two veteran agents in Virginia —one of whom is friends with a critic of President Trump —and punishing another in Las Vegas, according to several people familiar with the matter.

evidence_map.fact: The report named Spencer Evans, Stanley Meador and Michael Feinberg and described their FBI roles.
evidence_map.quote: Two of the men, Spencer Evans and Stanley Meador, are senior agents who ran F.B.I. field offices in Las Vegas and Richmond, Va. The third, Michael Feinberg, a top deputy in the Norfolk, Va., office, had ties to a former agent whom Kash Patel, the F.B.I. director, identified in his book as part of the so-called deep state.
evidence_map.source_excerpt: Two of the men, Spencer Evans and Stanley Meador, are senior agents who ran F.B.I. field offices in Las Vegas and Richmond, Va. The third, Michael Feinberg, a top deputy in the Norfolk, Va., office, had ties to a former agent whom Kash Patel, the F.B.I. director, identified in his book as part of the so-called deep state.

evidence_map.fact: The report said one agent resigned after a threatened demotion and two others were forced to move and retire.
evidence_map.quote: Threatened with demotion, a veteran agent with ties to a former official on the F.B.I. director’s so-called enemies list opted to resign. Two others were forced to move and retire.
evidence_map.source_excerpt: Threatened with demotion, a veteran agent with ties to a former official on the F.B.I. director’s so-called enemies list opted to resign. Two others were forced to move and retire.

evidence_map.fact: WRIC, relaying The New York Times, reports that Richmond FBI special agent in charge Stanley Meador was placed on administrative leave and expected to retire.
evidence_map.quote: The New York Times reports that Stanley Meador, special agent in charge of Richmond’s FBI field office, has been put on administrative leave and “was expected to retire.”
evidence_map.source_excerpt: The New York Times reports that Stanley Meador, special agent in charge of Richmond’s FBI field office, has been put on administrative leave and “was expected to retire.”

evidence_map.fact: WRIC attributes the characterization of the broader FBI personnel changes as retaliatory to current and former agents cited by The New York Times.
evidence_map.quote: “The wave of changes, current and former agents say, amount to little more than retaliation, underscoring what they describe as the politicization of the FBI as its leaders seek to mollify Mr. Trump’s supporters,” the New York Times said.
evidence_map.source_excerpt: “The wave of changes, current and former agents say, amount to little more than retaliation, underscoring what they describe as the politicization of the FBI as its leaders seek to mollify Mr. Trump’s supporters,” the New York Times said.

impact_proposal.confidence_reason: A New York Times report and local coverage establish a June FBI personnel episode, but the account relies on people familiar with the decisions and reports retaliation as an allegation.
impact_proposal.rationale: The sourced event concerns several named FBI officials facing personnel actions; the wider claim about eliminating oversight is not established.
impact_proposal.basis: Scores are provisional editorial estimates under impact-v2; source limitations prevent treating alleged retaliation as a finding.
impact_proposal.notes: The harms and institutional effects are bounded to reported personnel actions. A low procedural-abuse estimate reflects an attributed retaliation concern, not a legal finding; no private benefit is established.
